newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan's Lee accuses China of political coercion.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan's Lee accuses China of political coercion.

text.p: Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui on Saturday accused China of using commerce as a political weapon and urged local companies to exercise "restraint" over their mainland investments.

"Communist China is trying to use our people to coerce our government and use commerce to achieve political coercion in order to pressure our government," Lee told a meeting of Taiwan's top business leaders.
"Faced with this situation, we must uphold the principle of exercising restraint and avoiding rashness in order to handle the current cross-straits relations," he added.
Lee's comments came after Taiwan's top economic policymaker Chiang Ping-kun said on Friday that local firms should slow their pace of investment in China.
Lee himself said in August that Taiwan needed to review its policy of targeting China as its main market to avoid over-dependence.
This led to speculation that Taipei might attempt to curb the growing flow of investment to the mainland.
Taiwan and China have been rivals since a civil war divided them in 1949 and Beijing still regards the island as a renegade province.
Though all investments in China must be approved by the government, Taipei fears its economy could become too dependent on China -- and hence politically vulnerable.

Taipei has so far not tightened its policy of allowing businesses to invest in China through a third territory, but the recent cancellation of mainland projects by two major firms has raised concerns that the trade climate may be worsening.
Food giant President Enterprises announced on Thursday it had abandoned plans to build a US$100 million power plant in China because it had failed to reach agreement with mainland China counterparts.

On August 16, giant Formosa Plastics Group said it was ending a deal to build what would have been the biggest Taiwanese project in China to date, a US$3 billion power plant in coastal Fujian province.
Without directly mentioning the cancelled projects, Lee said China's unwillingness to resume talks with Taiwan was causing a general impasse.
"My offer for talks... is internationally considered the principle for furthering cross-straits relations. But communist China is intentionally neglecting the offer," Lee said.
He was referring to his proposal earlier this year to travel to China on a "journey of peace".

China angrily suspended semi-official talks in mid-1995 after Lee made a private but high-profile visit to the United States. Beijing claimed his visit showed Taiwan wanted independence rather than reunification with the mainland.

Both sides have expressed willingness to resume talks in recent months, but Beijing has stopped short of letting this happen, saying Taiwan should show sincerity by abandoning its its efforts to raise its international profile.
China threatens to attack Taiwan if the island tries to declare independence.
Some 30,000 Taiwanese companies have poured more than US$20 billion into China since a political thaw in the late 1980s.
